artifacts.synopsis: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

artifacts.synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.

artifacts.title: Dudt v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

artifacts.synopsis: A complaint challenging a session's refusal to advance an ordained deacon's nomination for re-election to the diaconate was denied by the SJC. Northwest Georgia Presbytery had adopted its judicial commission's judgment that the session did not err; applying BCO 39-3(3)'s deference to discretionary judgments, the SJC found no clear error, held formal charges were unnecessary and re-election was not guaranteed, and refused to attribute one elder's questionable retaliation rationale to the session. The majority encouraged prompt communication of reasons. A dissent would apply BCO 39-3.4 and sustain.

artifacts.title: Troxell v. Presbytery of the Southwest
artifacts.synopsis: A complaint challenged Presbytery’s institution of two charges against a teaching elder and related pretrial actions. The SJC annulled the household-management charge because process began fifteen months after the alleged offense and the record showed no recently flagrant, newly evident, or continuing offense under BCO 32-20. It also held that declaring the elder not in good standing removed rights without process, but left his properly imposed suspension effective. It rejected objections to discussion, questioning, and the timely submission charge, which could proceed without any determination of guilt.

artifacts.synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

artifacts.title: Flesher and Weekly v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: In Complaint 2015-03, Steve Flesher and Randy Weekly challenged Metro Atlanta Presbytery, but the SJC did not reach the merits. Because the issues raised had already been adjudicated in Appeal 2015-08, the SJC declared Complaint 2015-03 moot and approved that disposition. The short decision thus records a mootness ruling based on prior appellate adjudication; the underlying presbytery action and the Appeal 2015-08 decision are not described in the supplied text.

It reversed and dismissed the clerk-duty specification because the four-month delay in submitting minutes was attributable to the Session and did not justify a trial. artifacts.synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

artifacts.synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

artifacts.synopsis: The Standing Judicial Commission affirmed that Presbytery of Western Carolina did not err in conducting its BCO 31-2 investigation of accusations against TE Craig Bulkeley or in finding no strong presumption of guilt. The SJC found no constitutional error in Presbytery's procedures and gave great deference to the lower court's discretionary judgment, noting that BCO 31-2 does not mandate specific procedures for investigations. The SJC also held that complainants Kirk Lyons and Robert Woodward lacked standing to bring complaints under BCO 43-1 and 11-4.

artifacts.synopsis: Chastain appealed Heritage Presbytery’s 2006 excommunication and deposition. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order because Chastain had renounced PCA jurisdiction on May 8, 2006. Consequently, Presbytery’s later proceedings were moot and SJC 2005-1 remained in effect. The SJC did not reach the merits. A concurrence questioned the discipline process after renunciation; a dissent argued the majority lacked constitutional authority to recognize unilateral withdrawal and thereby undercut discipline.

artifacts.synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.
